issues.legal_issue: Joint family property retains its character when the coparcenary is temporarily reduced to one member while the joint family continues.
material_facts: The properties were ancestral property jointly held by two brothers.
After one brother died, the surviving brother became the sole surviving coparcener.
The deceased brother’s widow remained alive and had a right to maintenance from the joint family property.
issues.conclusion: The property did not cease to be joint family property merely because only one coparcener remained.
issues.legal_principle: A Hindu joint family may continue to exist despite having only one male coparcener, and its property does not become that coparcener’s separate property merely for that reason. The Court relied on Gowli Buddanna v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Mysore and Attorney General of Ceylon v. A. R. Arunachalam Chettiar.

predicates.joint_family_property: The property was held as property of a joint Hindu family.
predicates.coparcenary_reduced_to_one: The death of a family member left only one male coparcener.
predicates.widow_maintenance_right_continues: A widow of a deceased family member remained in the family and had a maintenance right against the property.

issues.definition: When joint family property remains in a family with a continuing maintenance right despite the coparcenary being reduced to one member, the property retains its joint family character.

issues.legal_issue: A child adopted by a widow becomes the child of her deceased husband and may become a coparcener in that husband’s joint family.
material_facts: The joint family property remained coparcenary property after the deceased brother’s widow’s husband died.
The widow adopted a son before the surviving coparcener died.
The surviving coparcener died after the adoption, and the adopted son claimed the joint family properties.

A will concerning the house was held valid as to half of the deceased surviving coparcener’s share, and the decree for the adopted son’s title to the agricultural land and half share of the house was restored.
issues.conclusion: The adopted son became the son of both the widow and her deceased husband, became a coparcener with the surviving brother, and, after that brother’s death, was entitled to the joint family properties subject to the will’s effect on the house.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 5, 6, 8, 11(vi) and 12 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, adoption transfers the child from the birth family to the adoptive family and replaces the child’s former family ties. Read with section 14, including its treatment of a widow who later marries, the scheme implies that a child adopted by a widow becomes the child of her deceased husband as well as of the widow. The Court relied on Arukushi Narayan v. Janabai Sama Sawat, and applied the principles concerning the continuing character of joint family property discussed in Gowli Buddanna and Attorney General of Ceylon v. A. R. Arunachalam Chettiar.

predicates.widow_adopted_child: A widow adopted a child into her family.
predicates.adopted_family_was_deceased_husbands_joi: The widow belonged to the joint family of her deceased husband into which the child was adopted.
predicates.joint_property_remained_coparcenary: The property at issue retained its character as coparcenary property when the adoption occurred.

issues.definition: If a widow adopts a child into her deceased husband’s continuing joint family while its property remains coparcenary property, the child becomes a coparcener in that family.

issues.legal_issue: The rights of an ordinary tenant are heritable when the governing tenancy law makes no special provision against heritability.
material_facts: The disputed agricultural land was held under ordinary tenancy rights.

The respondent argued that those rights were not heritable because the tenancy law had special provisions concerning the heritability of pakka tenants but no corresponding provision for ordinary tenants.
The Court considered the provisions governing ordinary tenants and mutation of names.
issues.conclusion: The ordinary tenancy rights were heritable, with heritability governed by the tenants’ personal law in the absence of a special statutory provision.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 86, 87 and 89 of the Madhya Bharat Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 1950 support the conclusion that ordinary tenancy rights are not excluded from heritability: section 87 concerns the terms on which an ordinary tenant holds land, while section 86 applies to holders of land generally and contemplates a new holder succeeding to a former holder’s title. In the absence of a special statutory rule, the personal law of the tenants governs heritability.

predicates.ordinary_tenancy: The land was held under ordinary tenancy rights rather than a distinct tenancy category with its own special rules.
predicates.tenancy_law_has_no_specific_heritability: The governing tenancy law contains no special rule making ordinary tenancy rights non-heritable.
predicates.personal_law_applies_to_tenant: The tenant’s personal law governs the inheritance of rights not specifically addressed by the tenancy law.

issues.definition: Ordinary tenancy rights are heritable when the governing tenancy law does not specifically exclude heritability and the tenant’s personal law applies.

issues.legal_issue: A contention against civil court jurisdiction cannot be raised in a later appeal when the lower courts decided it and it was not challenged in the intervening High Court appeal.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court decided the jurisdiction issue against the respondent.
The respondent did not challenge that decision in the High Court.
The respondent attempted to raise the jurisdiction issue in the Supreme Court appeal.
issues.conclusion: The respondent could not raise the jurisdiction contention at that stage.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the rule of appellate procedure that a party may not raise at a later appellate stage a lower-court ruling that the party did not challenge in the intervening appeal.

predicates.later_appeal_proceeding: A party sought to raise an issue in an appeal following an intervening appellate decision.
predicates.lower_courts_decided_jurisdiction_issue: The lower courts had decided the jurisdiction issue against the party seeking to raise it later.
predicates.jurisdiction_issue_not_challenged_in_int: The party did not challenge that decision in the intervening appeal.

issues.definition: A party cannot raise a jurisdiction contention in a later appeal when the lower courts decided it against that party and the party did not challenge it in the intervening appeal.
